intro:
By the end of this track you can explain what happens to a payment event from `send()` to the last consumer that reads it, and predict what each setting changes on the way. You will know a partition as an append-only log with one bookmark per reader, and build everything else on that picture: segments, retention and compaction; leaders, followers, the ISR and the high watermark; keys, batches, acks and idempotence; the poll loop, commits and rebalances; retries, dead letters and transactions; Kafka Streams tables and windows; schemas, Connect and change data capture; share groups, partition sizing and lag. Every lesson starts from a failure you could meet in a payments platform (a lost write, a double charge, a stuck partition) and ends with the setting or the pattern that prevents it.

You need to read Java and Kotlin, have JDK 21 or newer, and have Docker for the broker-backed tests and Try-its. Every code sample comes in both languages. The track assumes Apache Kafka 4.4: KRaft only, `linger.ms=5`, idempotence on by default, the new consumer protocol available but not the client default, share groups production-ready. No other track is required.

The labs live in `labs/kafka`, one package per lesson (`sfz.kafka.l01` to `l12`). Each lab is a small model of the mechanism (a log, an ISR, an accumulator, an assignor, a share partition) plus a client that the tests run against a real Kafka 4.4 broker started by Testcontainers, or against `TopologyTestDriver` and `MockConsumer` where no broker is needed. Run `./gradlew :kafka:test --tests 'sfz.kafka.l05.*'` from the `labs` folder. The Try-its use `labs/env/kafka.yml` (one broker on `localhost:9092`, with Schema Registry, PostgreSQL and Debezium behind profiles) and `labs/env/kafka-cluster.yml` (three brokers), and `./gradlew :kafka:demo -Pmain=...` for the demos.
cheatsheet:
## The model (lessons 1 and 2)

A topic is a set of partitions. A partition is an append-only log: the broker gives each record the next offset, offsets never change, and order exists only inside a partition. A reader's state is one number per partition, the offset of the next record; a group saves it in `__consumer_offsets` as its committed offset. Reading deletes nothing.

| On disk | Rule |
|---|---|
| Segment | files named by base offset (`.log`, `.index`, `.timeindex`); only the active segment takes appends; rolls at `segment.bytes` 1 GiB or `segment.ms` 7 days |
| Retention (`cleanup.policy=delete`) | deletes whole closed segments once their newest record is older than `retention.ms` (7 days) or the partition is over `retention.bytes`; the earliest offset jumps a segment at a time |
| Compaction (`cleanup.policy=compact`) | keeps at least the last record per key in closed segments; offsets and order never change; a tombstone (null value) deletes a key after `delete.retention.ms` (1 day) |
| Tiered storage | `remote.storage.enable=true`: closed segments go to object storage, `local.retention.ms` keeps the newest on disk; needs a plugin; no compacted topics |

## The cluster (lesson 3)

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| KRaft controllers | keep metadata in the Raft log `__cluster_metadata`; run 3 or 5; ZooKeeper is gone since 4.0 |
| Leader, followers | one leader per partition takes writes; followers fetch from it |
| ISR | replicas that keep up; a follower drops out after `replica.lag.time.max.ms` (30 s) or when its broker is fenced |
| High watermark | the smallest log end offset in the ISR; consumers read only below it |
| `acks=all` | waits for the current ISR, which can be the leader alone |
| `min.insync.replicas` | the floor for `acks=all` (default 1): below it writes fail with `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS`; use RF 3 and 2 for money |

## Producing (lessons 4 and 5)

- Partition of a keyed record: `(murmur2(key bytes) & 0x7fffffff) % partitions`. Same key, same partition, same order. Key payments by account id. Adding partitions moves most keys.
- No key: sticky runs of about `batch.size`, steered away from slow brokers (KIP-794).
- `send()` appends to a batch and returns a Future. A batch leaves when full (`batch.size` 16 KB) or old (`linger.ms` 5 ms since 4.0).
- Retries run on their own until `delivery.timeout.ms` (2 min). A `TimeoutException` means unknown, not unwritten.
- Idempotence (default): producer id plus sequence numbers; the leader drops duplicates of retries. It needs `acks=all`, retries and at most 5 in flight; `acks=1` turns it off silently.

## Consuming (lessons 6 to 8)

| Setting or fact | Value and meaning |
|---|---|
| Thread safety | one thread per consumer; only `wakeup()` may be called from another |
| Commit | the next offset to read: last processed + 1 |
| Commit after processing | at-least-once: duplicates after a crash, so dedupe with an idempotency key in the same database transaction |
| Commit before processing | at-most-once: a crash loses records |
| `auto.offset.reset` | `latest` by default for a group with no committed offset |
| `max.poll.records` / `max.poll.interval.ms` | 500 / 5 min: miss the interval and the member leaves the group |
| Rebalance | eager hands back everything; cooperative moves only what must move; KIP-848 (`group.protocol=consumer`, not the 4.4 client default) lets the broker assign and members reconcile alone |
| Liveness | session timeout 45 s for dead processes, `max.poll.interval.ms` for stuck loops; `group.instance.id` keeps partitions through a restart |
| Poison pill | blocks its partition: bounded retries for transient errors, a dead-letter topic with origin headers for permanent ones, park the key to keep per-account order |

## Exactly-once inside Kafka (lessons 9 and 10)

`transactional.id` + `initTransactions` (fences older epochs) + `beginTransaction` + sends + `sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, consumer.groupMetadata())` + `commitTransaction`. Records are in the log before the decision; COMMIT and ABORT markers take an offset. Readers need `isolation.level=read_committed` (default `read_uncommitted`) and stop at the last stable offset. After an abort, seek back. It covers Kafka writes and offsets only: calls and database writes still need idempotency keys (KIP-939 2PC hasn't shipped). Kafka Streams: `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2`.

## Kafka Streams (lesson 10)

KStream = events; KTable = latest value per key; `aggregate` folds a stream into a table, `toStream` lists its changes. State lives in RocksDB under `state.dir`, one slice per task (input partition), backed by `<application.id>-<store>-changelog` (compacted); a new owner restores from it; `num.standby.replicas=1` keeps a warm copy. Windows by event time; stream time = largest timestamp seen in a task; a window closes at end + grace. `group.protocol=streams` (KIP-1071, 4.2): broker-side task assignment. `errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name` (4.2).

## Schemas, Connect, CDC (lesson 11)

| Mode | Check | Upgrade first |
|---|---|---|
| BACKWARD (default) | new schema reads data of the latest | consumers |
| FORWARD | latest reads data of the new schema | producers |
| FULL | both | either |
| `_TRANSITIVE` | against every version | as above |

Wire format: byte 0, 4-byte schema id, Avro bytes. Avro: missing reader field takes its default, or fails. Connect: workers, connectors, tasks, converters, transforms; state in `connect-configs`, `connect-offsets`, `connect-status`. Outbox: business row + event row in one database transaction; Debezium reads the WAL through a replication slot, committed transactions in commit order, stores the LSN; at-least-once, dedupe on the event id.

## Share groups and operations (lesson 12)

| | Consumer group | Share group |
|---|---|---|
| Who reads a partition | one member | every member |
| Max useful members | partition count | no such cap |
| Progress | one committed offset per partition | a state per record: available, acquired, acknowledged, archived |
| Failure of one record | blocks the partition | RELEASE retries it, REJECT archives it; archived after 5 deliveries; DLQ to `dlq.*` in 4.4 |
| Order | per partition, per key | none |

Partitions: max(target / per-partition producer rate, target / per-consumer rate), plus growth. Lag: log end offset minus committed offset, per partition; alert on growth and on the age of the oldest record.
recap: A partition is an append-only log with offsets that never change, and each reader keeps one bookmark per partition; reading deletes nothing, and order exists only inside a partition.
Retention deletes whole segments by time or size; compaction keeps the latest record per key in closed segments. Neither touches the active segment.
A write is committed when the ISR has it. `acks=all` waits for the ISR, and `min.insync.replicas` sets how small the ISR may get: replication factor 3 with 2 for money.

The key picks the partition, so key payments by account and choose the partition count up front. The idempotent producer, on by default, stops retries from duplicating or reordering; it doesn't dedupe your own resends.

Commit after processing for at-least-once and make processing idempotent with an idempotency key. Rebalances move partitions and their bookmarks; commit on revoke, and prefer the new consumer protocol.
A record that always fails stops its partition: bounded retries, a dead-letter topic with origin headers, and a parked key keep the rest flowing in order.
Transactions make outputs and offsets one atomic write inside Kafka, for `read_committed` readers; anything outside Kafka still needs idempotency keys or an outbox.
Kafka Streams keeps tables and windows in local stores backed by compacted changelog topics; run `exactly_once_v2` when the state is money.
Schemas with a registry stop a producer from breaking consumers; BACKWARD means consumers upgrade first. The outbox plus Debezium turns a database commit into exactly the events it contains.
Share groups hand out records one by one with locks and delivery counts, giving queue semantics without order; size partitions from measured rates and watch lag per partition.

quiz.q: A topic has 6 partitions. Which group can usefully run 20 members, each processing a record at a time?
options: A consumer group: the broker splits each partition between members
A share group: every member reads every partition, and the broker hands out records one by one
Both, with `group.protocol=consumer`
Neither: 6 is the limit for any group
quiz.why: A consumer group gives each partition to one member, so 14 of 20 would sit idle, whatever the protocol. A share group has no such cap, at the price of order. The new consumer protocol changes how assignments are computed, not how many owners a partition has.

quiz.q: A payment consumer writes to Oracle and then commits its offset. It crashes between the two. What does the restart do, and what makes that safe?
options: It skips the payment; nothing is needed
It processes the payment again; the idempotent producer removes the duplicate
Nothing, because Kafka transactions cover the Oracle write
It processes the payment again; an idempotency key checked in the same Oracle transaction makes the repeat harmless
quiz.why: Committing after processing is at-least-once: the restart begins at the committed offset and repeats the payment. The idempotent producer only dedupes a producer's own retries, and a Kafka transaction covers Kafka writes and offsets, not Oracle. The consumer must recognise the repeat itself.

quiz.q: Which statement about retention and compaction is true?
options: Retention deletes single records once they expire
Compaction removes all but the last record per key in every segment, including the active one
Retention deletes whole closed segments; compaction keeps the last record per key in closed segments and never changes offsets
Compaction renumbers offsets so the log has no gaps
quiz.why: Both work on closed segments. Retention drops whole segments whose newest record is too old, so the earliest offset jumps a segment at a time. Compaction rewrites closed segments to keep the latest record per key, leaving gaps in the offsets; the active segment is never cleaned.

quiz.q: A topic has replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`. Two followers fall out of the ISR. What happens to a producer with `acks=all`?
options: Its writes fail with `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS`, retried until `delivery.timeout.ms`, then a `TimeoutException`
Its writes succeed: `acks=all` waits for the ISR, which is now just the leader
The leader waits for the followers to come back, without a timeout
The writes succeed but consumers can't read them
quiz.why: `acks=all` alone would accept the leader as the whole ISR. `min.insync.replicas` is the floor: with one in-sync replica and a floor of 2, the leader refuses the write. The producer retries a retriable error until its delivery timeout, then reports a `TimeoutException`, which means unknown, not lost.

quiz.q: A group of three consumers uses the classic protocol with the default assignor list, which starts with the eager Range assignor. A fourth member joins. What do the three existing members do?
options: Keep all their partitions; only the new member gets idle ones
Give up only the partitions that move to the new member
Give back all their partitions and wait for the new assignment
Leave the group and rejoin one at a time
quiz.why: Eager rebalancing revokes every partition from every member before reassigning, so all processing stops for the rebalance. The cooperative assignor revokes only what moves, in two rounds, and the KIP-848 protocol lets each member give up only its own moved partitions without a group-wide stop.

quiz.q: A producer has `acks=1` and doesn't set `enable.idempotence`. What happens to idempotence?
options: It stays on, the default since Kafka 3.0
It's turned off silently, because idempotence needs `acks=all`
The producer fails to start with a `ConfigException`
It stays on for retries but not for reordering
quiz.why: Idempotence is on by default only when nothing conflicts with it. `acks=1` conflicts, so the producer turns it off without a word. Only if you also set `enable.idempotence=true` explicitly does the conflict become a `ConfigException`.

quiz.q: A consume-transform-produce service uses transactions. A downstream consumer with default settings reads its output. What does it see after a batch is aborted?
options: Nothing from the aborted batch: aborted records are deleted
Only the ABORT marker
Nothing at all until `transaction.timeout.ms`
The aborted records too, because the default `isolation.level` is `read_uncommitted`
quiz.why: Transactional records are in the log before the decision, and an abort only adds a marker. Hiding aborted records is the reader's job, and only `read_committed` readers do it. Exactly-once inside Kafka needs every reader of the output to opt in.

quiz.q: A Kafka Streams balance app runs `at_least_once`. What does switching to `exactly_once_v2` change?
options: The output records, changelog writes and input offsets of each commit go into one transaction, so a crash can't count a payment twice
Nothing for state: changelogs were always exact
Kafka Streams stops using changelog topics
External API calls in the topology happen once
quiz.why: Under at-least-once, updates reach the changelog before the offsets are committed, so after a crash the restored store already contains payments that are then processed again. One transaction per commit ties them together. Calls outside Kafka are still not covered.

quiz.q: A subject is in BACKWARD mode. A team removes a field that had no default and adds one with a default. Which deploy order is safe?
options: Producers first, then consumers
Consumers first, then producers
Any order: the registry accepted it
Neither: the registry rejects both changes
quiz.why: BACKWARD accepts a schema that can read data written with the latest version: removed fields are skipped and the new field has a default, so it's accepted. It promises nothing about old consumers reading new data, so consumers move first, then producers. Removing a field without a default would fail under FORWARD.

quiz.q: Which of these is a job for a share group rather than a consumer group?
options: Applying each account's payments to the ledger in order
Building a running balance per account
Sending a webhook to a merchant for each settled payment, where each call is independent and slow
Replicating a compacted account topic into a cache
quiz.why: Share groups scale past the partition count and retry or archive each record on its own, but give up order. Independent, slow work items fit. The ledger and the balance need per-account order and state, and a compacted topic's latest-value-per-key replay needs a reader that walks each partition in order.
